newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl calls for "responsible" steel solution.
newsitem.headline: Kohl calls for "responsible" steel solution.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl called on Thursday for a "reasonable" solution to talks on a planned mammoth steel industry merger as fears grew that the deal would push Germany further down the road to mass unemployment.

But workers at steel giant Thyssen called off a strike after their own company and Krupp announced that they were embarking immediately on a week of talks which might make Krupp's planned hostile takeover of Thyssen superfluous.

The news suggested at least a temporary return to Germany's long-standing culture of industrial consensus in the face of spiralling unemployment, now over 12 percent, which has put Kohl under pressure as never before in his 14-year tenure.

There was also some respite for Kohl from the widely-watched Ifo index of the west German business climate, which edged up to a solid 93.6 in February, providing evidence that the gloom that has plagued the economy may be lifting.
But economists unanimously caution that growth does not mean job creation and that an upswing in the jobs market, rapidly becoming the issue that Kohl will stand or fall on, is far off.
Kohl urged both companies in a statement to "live up to their responsibilities".

"In the interest of those employed by both companies and in the interest of the economic climate in our country, the issue is to find a reasonable solution," said Kohl, who has only just managed to quell weeks of speculation about his own desire and ability to lead party and country.

The steel move, the brainchild of Krupp chief executive Gerhard Cromme, has angered workers threatened by layoffs and those who see mass unemployment across the densely populated coal-and-steel territory of the Ruhr Valley.
But it has also inflamed fears of a new era of cut-throat competition for scarce jobs and perhaps social unrest unknown in post-war Germany.
"Mr Cromme, do you want to set our country alight?" Wednesday's Bild, Germany's biggest selling daily, screamed across its front page.
Krupp and Thyssen said they would discuss merging their steel operations into a joint company, but Krupp cautioned that if these failed, it would go back to its takeover bid.
Analysts had said a full takeover would lead to 10,000 or more job losses, and it was not clear how many would be saved by a less comprehensive partial merger.

Either way, the upheaval could not have come at a worse time for job fears, after the government two weeks ago sparked outrage among Germany's miners by announcing a multi-billion mark cut in long-standing subsidies to the collieries.
Three days of miners' demonstrations in Bonn and a week of marches in Berlin by construction workers facing mass layoffs forced Kohl to offer financial concessions to both.
Those confrontations also added to the impression that his ability to foster agreement between industry and workers in the interests of all was in shreds.

While economists say there is no alternative to more restructuring and rationalisation to adapt the German economy to the challenge of global markets, most commentators lament the impending loss of the consensus culture Kohl stands for.
"This hostile takeover is a sign of how raw the social climate has become around here. Social conditions, jobs and tradition don't matter, profit does," commented North German Radio.

"The politicians have contributed to that by throwing their weight entirely behind market forces, declined to steer economic development and made the dogmas of performance and competition the centre of their economic policy."
